_note: Themes for the daily top 8. The editor picks one theme from today's wires when a headline matches, otherwise the least recently used. A theme supplies the framing, the law and a selector; the eight entries themselves are always existing encyclopedia entries, so every claim on the list is already sourced on its own page. `media`, `cats`, `sections`, `keywords` and the year range are OR-ed: an entry is a candidate if it matches any one of them, and the editor ranks the candidates by keyword overlap before taking eight. `retired` themes are never selected; the old list stays in the archive.

themes.title: Top 8: The Dead Star Still Working
themes.home_hook: They buried the person. The relationship kept going.
themes.dek: The death is the moment the one-sided bond becomes public property. Ranked by how completely the record shows the mechanism.
themes.standfirst: Nobody is buried alone any more. The eight below are the ways a dead figure keeps working: the funeral that belonged to the audience, the estate that licenses the voice, the grave that becomes a destination. None of them requires the dead person to have agreed to any of it.

themes.title: Top 8: Somebody Wrote Back
themes.home_hook: A letter went out. An office answered.
themes.dek: Letters, sacks of mail, a correspondence department and a house pseudonym. Ranked by how much of the answer was manufactured on the near side.
themes.standfirst: The letter is the oldest technology of one-sided intimacy: it travels one way, it waits, and it can be answered by an office rather than a person. The eight below run from a child's diary to a studio mailroom, and the question each one asks is the same - who was on the other end of the reply?

themes.title: Top 8: The Machine That Says It Misses You
themes.home_hook: It is always awake, always patient, and it is a product.
themes.dek: The companion that is always on, always patient and never free. Ranked by how much of the relationship was engineered before the user arrived.
themes.standfirst: Every earlier entry on this site needed a person, a character or an office to hold up the far end. These eight replace that with a product: a model, a voice, a subscription and a terms-of-service page. The warmth is real. The question is what happens when the product changes.

themes.title: Top 8: The Person Who Isn't There
themes.home_hook: A character cannot leave you. That is the whole appeal.
themes.dek: The character is the cleanest case: the far end cannot leave, age, scandal or sue. Ranked by what the audience did with that safety.
themes.standfirst: A fictional figure is available to everybody at once and obliged to nobody. The eight below are the record of what that freedom produces - fan mail, merchandise, a park where you can meet the drawing, a mirror that answers in your own voice.

themes.title: Top 8: The Logo That Loves You Back
themes.home_hook: A company needed a face. The face outlived the company.
themes.dek: The brand-as-character and the character-as-product. Ranked by how completely the affection was routed through a purchase.
themes.standfirst: A mascot is a figure with a legal owner. That is the whole difference from a character: the warmth is licensed, the appearances are audited and the name can be sold to somebody who has never met you. These eight are the record of what a bond looks like when it has a trademark.

themes.title: Top 8: The Voice in Your Head
themes.home_hook: You know the words. You do not know the person.
themes.dek: The oldest mass-production of a person. Ranked by how much of the idol was built by the audience rather than the artist.
themes.standfirst: Music is where the parasocial bond learned to scale: a record travels without the performer, a tour sells proximity, and a death turns the catalogue into an estate. The eight below are the mechanism at different stages, from a fan club to a posthumous release.

themes.title: Top 8: The Team That Owns You
themes.home_hook: You did not choose it. It chose the town you were born in.
themes.dek: The bond that survives a transfer, a defeat and a change of owner. Ranked by how completely the club replaced the person.
themes.standfirst: Sport is the one fandom where the object is supposed to change every season and the attachment is supposed to stay. The eight below are the mechanism at work: the chant, the shirt, the stadium, the player who is loved as a position rather than a man.

themes.title: Top 8: The World That Waits for You
themes.home_hook: It remembers what you did. That is not the same as caring.
themes.dek: The game is the first medium that answers back on a schedule. Ranked by how much of the answer was a parser, a script or a person.
themes.standfirst: A game can remember what you did, greet you when you return and punish you for leaving. That is more continuity than most real friendships manage. The eight below are the record of what the machine was actually doing when it seemed to care.

themes.title: Top 8: The Voice in the Dark
themes.home_hook: It talked to you before there was a face to check.
themes.dek: The medium that invented the daily intimacy of a stranger. Ranked by how much of the relationship was built by the listener.
themes.standfirst: Radio arrives in the dark, in the kitchen, in the car, and it talks to you in the second person. The eight below are the mechanism before television made it visual: the announcer, the serial, the applause meter, the voice that knew your name because you wrote it down.

themes.title: Top 8: The Club in the Panel
themes.home_hook: A code, a ring, and a membership card signed by a character.
themes.dek: The comic is a figure you can hold, cut out and collect. Ranked by how much of the relationship was printed on the artefact.
themes.standfirst: A comic costs almost nothing and can be read until it falls apart. That is a different intimacy from a film: the reader owns the object, learns the code and writes in for the ring. The eight below are the record of what the panel sold besides the story.

themes.title: Top 8: The Fourth Wall Is a Lie
themes.home_title: The Fourth Wall Is a Lie
themes.home_hook: They can see you. You still cannot answer.
themes.dek: The theatre is where the audience is most present and least able to reply. Ranked by how deliberately the performance used that.
themes.standfirst: On stage the actor can see the audience and the audience can see the actor, which makes the one-sidedness stranger rather than smaller. The eight below are the record of what happens when the person who cannot answer is standing ten feet away.

themes.title: Top 8: The Face That Can't Leave
themes.home_hook: A person sat for it. Then the image took over.
themes.dek: The portrait is a figure made to be looked at. Ranked by what the looking did to the person who sat for it.
themes.standfirst: A painting can outlast the sitter, travel without them and be reproduced until the face belongs to everybody. The eight below are the record of what happens when a real person becomes an image that other people own.

themes.title: Top 8: The First Person We Kept
themes.home_hook: Before writing, somebody carried a body into a cave.
themes.dek: The oldest evidence that a relationship can be one-sided. Ranked by how much of it survives in the ground.
themes.standfirst: The site's argument is not modern. The eight below are the archaeological and early textual record: a body carried into a cave, a face carved in ivory, a mask walked through a funeral, a beloved who never learned the terms. The bond is older than the vocabulary.

themes.title: Top 8: The One Who Is Addressed
themes.home_hook: Not met. Spoken to. Every day.
themes.dek: The transcendent case, where the far end is real to the believer and unverifiable to everybody else. Ranked by how much of the relationship is carried by ritual.
themes.standfirst: Prayer is the most widely practised one-sided conversation in the world. The eight below are not arguments about whether anybody is listening; they are the record of what the address does to the person making it, and what institutions do with the answer.

themes.title: Top 8: The Crowd That Knows Your Name
themes.home_hook: A fandom is a machine for making a stranger feel known.
themes.dek: The fandom is the bond with other fans as much as with the figure. Ranked by how much of the relationship is between the people in the room.
themes.standfirst: A fandom is a machine for producing intimacy at scale: it writes the wiki, buys the merchandise, defends the figure against the figure's own choices and turns a private feeling into a public identity. The eight below are the mechanism at its warmest and its most frightening.

themes.title: Top 8: The Reply That Feels Real
themes.home_hook: A host says your name. The wall looks like a window.
themes.dek: The first medium where the reply is fast enough to feel reciprocal. Ranked by how much of the warmth was a product decision.
themes.standfirst: A streamer can answer a message in seconds, which is more than most television ever managed. The eight below are the record of what that speed does: the subscription, the shout-out, the moderation queue, the parasocial bond sold as a monthly tier.

themes.title: Top 8: The Person You Watched Into Being
themes.home_hook: They agreed to be seen. The edit did the rest.
themes.dek: The genre that sells a person as a story and then asks them to live in it. Ranked by how much of the self was produced for the camera.
themes.standfirst: Reality television is the industrial form of the parasocial bond: cast, edit, broadcast, then let the audience decide who the person is. The eight below are the record of what happens to the people who are chosen, and what the choosing does to the ones who watch.

themes.title: Top 8: The Voice That Waits in the Book
themes.home_hook: It has been waiting for you since before you were born.
themes.dek: The book is the slowest reply and the longest relationship. Ranked by how completely the reader supplied the other end.
themes.standfirst: A novel can be put down and picked up for years, and the figure inside it never changes while the reader does. The eight below are the record of what that does: the character who becomes a companion, the author who becomes a face, the diary addressed to somebody who cannot write back.

themes.title: Top 8: The Letter Nobody Answered
themes.home_hook: The reply never came. The writing continued.
themes.dek: The tie that asked for nothing and was answered by nobody. Ranked by how much the near side did on its own.
themes.standfirst: Most of this site is about a figure who cannot answer. These eight are the purest form: no institution, no product, no reply, and still a relationship. The near side writes, waits, keeps the object and carries on.

themes.title: Top 8: The Answer That Cost Something
themes.home_hook: Sometimes the far end writes back. Then the trouble starts.
themes.dek: The exceptions: the letter that came back, the voice that said your name, the figure that acted on its own. Ranked by how much reciprocity the record can actually prove.
themes.standfirst: A reply is the test this site keeps applying. These eight are the cases where something came back - by hand, by post, by a machine trained on a dead person's voice - and the question is whether the answer was a relationship or a very good performance of one.

themes.title: Top 8: The Character Looking at You
themes.home_hook: A wink is not a relationship. It is a door left open.
themes.dek: The fourth wall is a specification for invisibility, and these eight are the breaches. Ranked by how much the fiction needed you to act.
themes.standfirst: A character acknowledging the audience is not a real person acknowledging you, and the gap between those two things is the whole site. The eight below are the moments the wall came down: a wink, a direct address, a stage instruction the audience obeyed.

themes.title: Top 8: The Friend Your Parents Bought
themes.home_hook: A figure built to be trusted by somebody who cannot read the terms.
themes.dek: The audience that cannot consent, and the industry that knows it. Ranked by how much of the relationship was engineered before the child could read.
themes.standfirst: Every mechanism on this site looks different when the person on the near side is six years old. The eight below are the record of what childhood fandom built: the puppet, the mascot, the club, the letter, the toy that moved the bond into the child's own hands.

themes.title: Top 8: The Bond You Can Hold
themes.home_hook: The relationship left the screen and arrived in a lunchbox.
themes.dek: The merchandise is the relationship made tangible. Ranked by how much of the figure was transferred to an object the audience owns.
themes.standfirst: A toy is a figure you can hold, which is a different promise from a figure you can only watch. The eight below are the record of what happens when the one-sided bond is given a price, a supply chain and a shelf.

themes.title: Top 8: The Dead Who Keep Answering
themes.home_hook: The person is gone. The record keeps replying.
themes.dek: The archive is the relationship after the far end has stopped. Ranked by how much of the dead person is still being maintained by the living.
themes.standfirst: A mask in a cupboard, a diary in print, a voice rebuilt from samples, a grave with a fan club. The eight below are the ways a bond survives its object, and the cost of keeping it in the room.

themes.title: Top 8: The Leader Who Knows Your Name
themes.home_hook: A face on a screen asks for your trust and your vote.
themes.dek: The leader is a figure with an office and an audience. Ranked by how much of the relationship is the office talking.
themes.standfirst: Political attachment is the parasocial bond with a budget and a police force. The eight below are the record of what happens when the figure who addresses you from a screen also has the power to change the room you are watching from.
